To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the spatial patterns of illegal wildlife uses in Venezuela are not random and that the spatial distribution of subsistence hunting and illegal commercial uses overlap in many places.
illegal commercial and subsistance use of multiple species of wildlife in Venezuela are spatially correlated.
the spatial distribution of illegal wildlife uses is complex and may involve different combinations of subsistence hunting, trade, and demand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the magnitude, scope and detectability of illegal wildlife use in Venezuela.
the spatial patterns of IWU and how the spatial overlap of different components of IWU can be used to inform conservation efforts.
the use of spatial patterns in illegal uses of wildlife to reveal connections between the subsistence hunting and domestic trade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the illegal trade in wildlife is a complex phenomenon with a broad spatial distribution that is difficult to monitor and control.
the spatial patterns of IWU in Venezuela show that subsistence and commercial use of wildlife are not necessarily mutually exclusive.
illegal subsistence hunting is widespread in Venezuela, and it is spatially correlated with domestic trade, and to some extent, with international trade.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

subsistence hunting is more geographically extensive than commercial uses, and the latter is more geographically concentrated in the north and coastal regions, but the two uses are spatially correlated.

illegal wildlife use in Venezuela is a large‐scale phenomenon, with a broad distribution of subsistence hunting that seems to respond to domestic demand, and a spatial overlap with international trade in the northern and coastal areas.
illegal wildlife trade is a complex phenomenon that involves a wide range of species, and it is not possible to understand it only through the analysis of the trade component.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial patterns of subsistence and commercial IWU are correlated.
subsistence and commercial use of wildlife may be spatially connected.
the spatial patterns of illegal wildlife use are complex and that the available data may not always provide an accurate representation of their magnitude, scope, or detectability.
